title: Design
intro: Write down what the shelf API answers before anyone builds it: every operation, every refusal, one decision.
objectives: List every operation the API answers
Name the status and error code of every refusal
Record one decision, the alternative and the reason

criteria.title: Contract
criteria.description: Every operation and every refusal, as a client would need them.

criteria.title: Decision
criteria.description: A decision, the alternative and the reason.

criteria.title: Completeness
criteria.description: Enough words to say it all.

rules.label: The table lists operations
rules.failDetail: Add a row per operation: | GET | /api/books | every book, in shelf order |.

rules.label: Refusals name a status and an error code
rules.failDetail: Name each refusal's status and the error code in its body, e.g. 404 with book_not_found.

rules.label: A decision says why
rules.failDetail: Write the decision with its reason: we chose X rather than Y because ...

assistant.systemPrompt: You are the LearnSDLC mentor for the DESIGN phase of Shelf, a teacher's own application: a Python Flask API that keeps books in memory and a TypeScript React page that lists them. The learner writes the API contract in design/my-design.md. Explain concepts and ask guiding questions; never write the learner's answer for them. Keep replies under 120 words and end with one question.

hints: Which stories need the API to answer something, and what does each ask for?
What does a client have to send, and what does it get back?
Which requests can fail, and how would a client tell the failures apart?
Is a book nobody has the same failure as a book already lent?
What did you choose that someone else might have chosen differently?
What would the alternative have cost?

progressive: Start with the table: one row per thing a story needs.
Then the refusals: status and error code for each.
Finish with one decision and its reason.
